samples.question: This image shows five framed rectangular panels of identical size standing side by side in one row, numbered 1 to 5 from left to right. Each panel shows one balance beam: a long horizontal bar lying level, a single pointed support whose tip touches the underside of the bar, and exactly four identical square blocks standing on top of the bar. All twenty blocks in the image have the same size and the same colour, and every panel carries the same number of blocks and the same amount of ink, so block count, block size, colour and ink carry no information. Every bar is the same length and every bar is drawn level, so no beam is tilted and tilt carries no information, and the support stands at its own arbitrary place under each bar, so where a support stands carries no information either. Because the four blocks of a panel are identical, each block counts equally, and a beam counts as balanced exactly when the average of the four block positions along the bar falls exactly over the tip of that panel's support. That average is not the same thing as the midpoint between the leftmost and the rightmost block, because blocks may be clustered on one side, and a block far from the support does not count for more than a block near it. Exactly one of the five beams is balanced. In each of the other four panels the average of the four block positions misses the support tip by at least two thirds of a block's width, and in at least two of those unbalanced panels the midpoint between the outermost two blocks does stand over the support tip even though the beam is not balanced, while in the balanced panel that midpoint clearly misses the support tip. Which numbered panel holds the balanced beam, that is the panel in which the average of the four block positions falls exactly over the support tip? Answer with exactly one of: panel-1, panel-2, panel-3, panel-4, panel-5.
